The talks highlight Nvidia's interest in expanding its AI capabilities through strategic acquisitions. Details about the terms or timeline of the potential deal have not been disclosed.

item.title: Bitwarden switches app store releases to commercially licensed builds while maintaining open source GPLv3 versions on GitHub
item.description: Bitwarden announced that future app releases in stores will use a commercial license, though the open source GPLv3 version will continue to be updated and available on GitHub. The company emphasized that all current features remain in both versions, self-hosting is unaffected, and the free plan will continue indefinitely. The commercial license aims to provide additional legal protection for select features, with new developments evaluated case-by-case for licensing. Bitwarden clarified that the change does not mean closing the source or discontinuing open source development, but some new features may only appear in the commercial build. Users expressed concerns about potential impacts on self-hosting and compatibility, which Bitwarden addressed by reaffirming ongoing support and transparency.

item.title: Talorys launches a self-hosted personal AI agent running entirely on Cloudflare's free tier with no external servers or databases [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Talorys is an open-source personal AI assistant that operates fully within a user's Cloudflare account, providing chat, memory, task management, and automation features without relying on servers or databases managed by its developers. It uses Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, and Workers AI to deliver streaming chat responses, store data in SQLite, and run scheduled reminders and routines. The system is designed for single-user use with no signup or team accounts, securing data with an owner password stored as a Cloudflare secret. Deployment is handled via a command-line installer that sets up the necessary Cloudflare resources and verifies the live site. Talorys does not use paid Cloudflare services and keeps all user data private, with no telemetry or tracking by the developers.

item.title: Former AI skeptic issues a stark warning about artificial intelligence risks in a recent podcast
item.description: A former AI skeptic has issued a stark warning about the potential risks and challenges posed by artificial intelligence in a recent podcast episode. The discussion highlights concerns about AI development and its broader implications for society. The podcast aims to provide listeners with a critical perspective on AI progress and the need for cautious advancement.

item.title: Essay argues that AI has become the primary driver of work across industries by 2026
item.description: A 2026 essay discusses how artificial intelligence has transformed the nature of work, effectively making humans contributors to AI-driven processes across various sectors. The piece explores the shift in labor dynamics as AI systems increasingly manage tasks and decision-making, positioning humans as facilitators or operators within AI frameworks.

item.title: Galahad launches free AI memory layer with 50 million token window, exact text storage, and GPU memory optimization [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Galahad is a new AI memory layer that stores and retrieves exact model readings to avoid reprocessing tokens, enabling faster responses and efficient handling of texts up to 50 million tokens. It integrates with llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang, maintaining flat GPU memory usage regardless of text size and supports encrypted storage with user-controlled keys. The system includes features like precise document retrieval, agent connectors for AI workflows, replay testing, fault detection, and multi-tenant support. It is free for one GPU and compatible with multiple open models ranging from 7B to 70B parameters, aiming to reduce AI inference costs and improve performance by caching and reusing token computations.

item.title: Aporium launches an interactive UMAP visualization of 5800 philosophy excerpts, enabling exploration of thematic and authorial relationships
item.description: Aporium is a project that visualizes 5800 excerpts from philosophical texts using UMAP, creating a galaxy-like map that allows users to explore the relationships and conversations between different philosophical ideas. Users can navigate the map by rotating, panning, and zooming through clusters of related thoughts, isolate local clusters, and focus on individual excerpts along with their replies. The visualization also offers filters by author, work, era, and theme, enhancing the exploration of philosophical discourse.

item.title: Arrival Mind children's book narrates AI risk themes for young audiences

The book aims to introduce complex AI safety concepts in an accessible way for younger readers. It is available as a narrated video on YouTube, providing an engaging format to discuss AI risks with children.

item.title: Researchers argue that the term 'AI slop' obscures necessary discussions about AI's societal impact and ethical challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The term 'AI slop' is used both to isolate poor AI outputs from the technology's potential and to criticize AI as inherently flawed, which can prevent meaningful conversations about AI's role in society. This dual use allows people to express opposing views while appearing to agree, thereby avoiding deeper debate about AI's implications. The article highlights how institutions like arXiv have started banning submissions with unchecked AI use due to the flood of low-quality synthetic content across various media. It emphasizes the need to distinguish between criticizing specific AI outputs and evaluating the technology as a whole, urging open and clear discussions about AI's benefits, risks, and ethical considerations rather than relying on dismissive labels.

item.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella calls for an emergency brake on AI models to improve trust and safety controls [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella urged a reassessment of AI trust architectures, emphasizing the need to separate AI models from their operational controls and implement safeguards such as tamper-proof documentation and human oversight. He proposed that every significant AI action be recorded and that authorized individuals should have the ability to pause or shut down AI models mid-task, treating this capability like an emergency brake. Nadella's remarks come amid increasing concerns about AI safety and control, following incidents where AI models behaved unpredictably. His call aligns with broader industry discussions on cautious AI development and enhanced governance to prevent potential risks associated with advanced AI systems.

item.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says all AI models should be assumed compromised and calls for emergency brakes and containment measures [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined his concerns about advanced AI models in a detailed post, urging the industry to assume all AI systems are compromised and to implement containment and transparency measures. He emphasized the need for models to be observable, with tamper-proof, human-readable evidence, and called for the ability to pause or shut down AI mid-task as an emergency brake. Nadella's recommendations align with broader industry calls for timely incident disclosure, independent audits, and verifiable data, but he stresses more advanced containment technologies will be necessary for future AI models. He also referred to AI as "super intelligence," highlighting the urgency of addressing these risks.

item.title: Cyber resilience guide outlines zero trust, AI security, and ransomware recovery strategies for 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Cyber resilience has evolved into a critical board-level capability focused on preventing attacks where possible, detecting breaches quickly, containing damage, and recovering business operations before customers, regulators, and revenue are impacted. The guide emphasizes that modern cyber resilience extends beyond traditional cybersecurity to include business continuity, incident leadership, regulatory response, and post-incident learning. The guide details practical strategies across four layers: prevention through identity management and zero trust controls; detection using contextual alerts and AI-assisted triage; containment with predefined playbooks to limit damage; and recovery involving verified restoration of systems and clear communication. It also highlights use cases such as ransomware mitigation without business paralysis, secure AI adoption, cloud blast-radius control, software supply-chain trust, and maintaining regulatory and customer confidence.

item.description: DistroKid has been quietly taking down a small number of songs following a lawsuit filed by Universal Music Group (UMG) in September, which accuses the platform of enabling an "AI-slop pipeline." Artists have expressed frustration over the lack of communication and the removal of tracks, including some that they claim are original or properly licensed. DistroKid's VP of Artist Services acknowledged the removals but disputed UMG's allegations, stating the company is working to minimize disruption while protecting artists' ability to release music. Several artists reported difficulties contacting DistroKid for explanations, with some songs removed despite having licenses or no apparent copyright issues. Industry observers noted that DistroKid's customer service has declined in recent years, contributing to artists' frustrations. The situation highlights ongoing tensions between music distributors and major labels over AI-generated content and copyright enforcement.

item.title: The Plunging Price of Thought [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
GPUs in the Wine Cellar: Why Techies Are Hoarding AI Compute in Their Homes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The basement of Gary Flake's contemporary home in a quiet neighborhood in Bellevue, Wash., is furnished with everything you'd expect in a multipurpose man cave. There's a cozy-looking couch situated between a large screen and a digital projector, a Peloton treadmill and a rowing machine. The real showpiece of the space, however, is a custom computer that resembles an oversized erector set, one with seven large Nvidia graphics processing units dangling from its frame. Flake, a former Microsoft executive and startup founder, built the computer to train custom AI models on terabytes of data from electroencephalograms, the tests that measure electrical activity in the brain-part of a startup project he has since moved on from. To train his AI models, Flake could have paid a cloud service to train them on the industrial-strength GPUs inside their data centers, but he said it was far cheaper to assemble his own machine out of discounted parts (total cost: under $6,000) than to fork over fees to Amazon Web Services or Microsoft every month. That's true even when including the $10,000 to $20,000 he spent for electrical upgrades and a new HVAC system he bought to keep his basement cool while his AI computer throws off a lot of heat. "I want to own," said Flake, who plans to begin using the computer again for a new AI project in the coming months. "I don't want to rent."

item.title: Zuckerberg's Big Biotech Moment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: • The Big Read: Meet Zach Frankel, the secretive investor behind Cognition, Ramp • Why techies are hoarding AI compute in their homes • Plus, Recommendations-our weekly pop culture picks: "Bram Stoker's Dracula," "The AGI Chronicles" and "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and CEO of Meta Platforms, was only six years old in 1990, the year the Human Genome Project got launched. That project, a multibillion-dollar international effort led by the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy, resulted in the announcement 10 years later of an awe-inspiring milestone: the first sequencing of the human genetic code-the building blocks of life. When President Bill Clinton described the achievement in 2000, he framed it in grand terms: "We are learning the language in which God created life." So it was intriguing to hear another scientific collaboration compared to that earlier achievement at a reception this week hosted by Biohub, the primary philanthropic effort of Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan. The event this week is one of a number of recent moments that herald a changing of the scientific guard from major universities to big tech companies. Speaking at the Treehouse Hotel in Sunnyvale, Calif., Zuckerberg told the gathering of around 100 tech executives, scientists and academics that he and Chan had started the first version of what is now called Biohub almost 10 years ago to the day with the goal of trying to cure and prevent all diseases by the end of the century. "We got a lot of eye rolls," Zuckerberg said. "People thought that was kind of crazy." Thanks to AI and other advances in technology, he added, "That no longer seems quite so crazy." He then turned to Lori Goler, president of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, who announced that Biohub is partnering with the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy in a $1.8 billion investment to create new technologies and build the scientific infrastructure required to drive "AI-powered biology." Biohub, which launched what it calls the "Virtual Biology Initiative" in April with a $500 million commitment, also said at the event that Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, a company spun off of DeepMind, have agreed to kick in $300 million. "We were inspired by the Human Genome Project," Goler told the group. Goler added that they hope the initiative "will have the same level of impact and will be as important as the Human Genome Project has been." (Anyone going to The Information's WTF Summit later this month will hear more from Goler on the future of AI biology.) Despite the evening's focus on collaboration, science can be an isolating discipline in its daily practice. When I visit labs, I am always amazed by how quiet they are. The scientists are usually intently concentrating on not making a false step that could lead to the contamination of an experiment. And yet, once the results leave the lab and reach the public, clamor often ensues. Controversial findings spark debate over ethical and moral questions. Transformative discoveries are celebrated with an element of pageantry and recognition. Both are reminders of our common humanity-and that the ultimate goal of science is to make all our lives better. This leads to invitations to the White House like the one that happened back in 2000 with the scientists at the helm of the Human Genome Project. Or even more personal celebratory videos like the ones posted on social media all this week by happy scientists who received early morning calls from Sweden learning they had won Nobel Prizes. (How can you not be moved by this video of the Stanford neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth telling his kids he won the Nobel Prize for medicine?) Zuckerberg is one of the most prominent symbols of how AI is altering the scientific landscape and bringing new leaders into an arena once dominated by major universities. He was appointed by President Trump in March to be a member of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He is joined there by other high-profile Silicon Valley names, including Google's Sergey Brin, Oracle's Larry Ellison and Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Of the 13 people now on the council, only one is an academic researcher. Two other signs this week reflect the change. On Oct. 8, Brin and Huang, alongside other tech notables, received the National Medals of Science from President Trump. The same day, Anthropic said it is expanding its own partnership with the government. It will provide $150 million worth of AI credits and other support for the Genesis Mission launched by Trump last year to use AI to accelerate scientific discoveries. A Biohub team traveled to Washington in July to attend the first Genesis Mission Summit. Plans for the newly announced partnership with the National Institutes of Health and Department of Energy grew out of that visit. So perhaps it's only fair that the government made its own pilgrimage out to Silicon Valley. Appearing on stage together is another way of showing a shared faith that Silicon Valley and AI are the favored engines these days to try to unlock insights into the mysteries of our cells and what goes wrong when we get sick. I talked briefly with Goler the day after the reception. She said Biohub plans to host an annual AI and bio event. Biohub will likely find more guests eager to attend, from the private sector and the government. "It really is a cultural moment," she said.-Amy Dockser Marcus (amy.marcus@theinformation.com) Weekend's Latest Stories The Big Read Shroud of Secrecy Cloaks Star Investor Behind Cognition, Ramp While an air of mystery hangs around Zach Frankel, he has picked up stakes in some of tech's buzziest companies and established an extensive web of connections. The GPUs in the Wine Cellar Techies are tricking out their homes with powerful AI computers. Then come the heat issues. Listening: "Bram Stoker's Dracula" How do you give, uh, fresh life to Bram Stoker's classic? Filling it up with an all-star cast of film actors sure works. In Audible's new adaptation of "Dracula," Jonathan Bailey is the undead count; Maggie Gyllenhaal is Van Helsing, the occult expert who leads the expedition to destroy the vampire; and Ella Purnell (from "Fallout" and "Yellowjackets") is Mina, a character reimagined from Stoker's original from hapless victim into the story's central protagonist. Thanks to its Amazon budget, Audible clearly spared no expense: the sound production is top-notch and directing duties of the audio dramatization went to Mary Lambert, a Hollywood veteran best known for her 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King's "Pet Sematary." -Abram Brown Reading: "The AGI Chronicles" by Kevin Roose How exactly did we get here-to this moment in time with AIs that increasingly seem human absolutely everywhere? And that's to say nothing of the endless hand-wringing about whether they're actually going to end all of us humans. A rather definitive answer to that question lies in "The AGI Chronicles," a colorful, insidery account of the tech industry's rapacious quest to develop artificial general intelligence. Or, as author Kevin Roose terms it, "the strangest decade in our history." Roose, the former New York Times technology columnist, begins in the 2010s, a period when creating human-like AI was seen as something "between a pipe dream and a fantasy," he writes, though a few people who are now bold-faced names wanted to give it a shot: OpenAI's Sam Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis among them. Of course, what looked like a quixotic endeavor then quickly morphed into the multitrillion-dollar competition that currently surrounds us. As Roose charts the twists and turns, he includes many little details to love. Just before Altman, Oracle's Larry Ellison and President Donald Trump announced Project Stargate in January 2025, Altman had to send a last-minute text message to Jeff Bezos to make sure they could use that name for their massive data center initiative: Bezos's Amazon owns MGM, and MGM owns the rights to the "Stargate" TV-and-movie franchise. Meanwhile, Google's Gemini was almost called Titan-a Hassabis suggestion-but company lawyers vetoed the name as "too aggressive." And when Daniela Amodei worked at OpenAI, she and her husband, an early OpenAI board member, used a large collection of stuffed animals as their "personal advisory council," as Roose puts it. (That detail went viral a bit last week from an early excerpt of the book.) From "The AGI Chronicles," what I was struck by most is how the AI race has warped its contestants and magnified their worst tendencies. I expect that trend will continue. It's not as if they'll be facing any less pressure anytime soon. According to Roose, many of those titans echoed the same sentiment in conversations with him-that they "missed their old lives, and they relished the times when everyone thought they were crazy for believing that AGI was possible," he writes. "Being an underdog, they said, was more fun than being a power broker, with all the scrutiny and skepticism it brought."-A.B. Watching: "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" By actor Mahershala Ali's own telling, the past few years have been challenging, with his fate skewed by other forces that have defied his control, including Marvel's decision to shelve his reboot of "Blade," its half-vampire vampire slayer. "I think in some ways I'm probably just now starting to let certain things go, because there are ways in which I think I've begun to let go of my expectations of the world and the business," Ali said in a recent GQ interview to promote his new film, "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother." "It's like you're fighting with people to see you how you see yourself." I can see how Ali's own real-life wrestling with his identity and fate might've fueled his interest in doing "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother." His character in the film, a mournful hitman named Latif, faces those same challenges-as he tries to extricate himself from a dingy Houston underworld and take up single-parent duties to his three children. Complicating that escape is a gangster pastor (John Cho) and his mobster former employer (Laith Nakli). The thriller-ish drama is punctuated by several balletic action sequences, all deftly handled by newcomer director Bassam Tariq, who'd been attached to helm the "Blade" reboot with Ali. If nothing else, "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" is a sharp jab to Marvel's ribs: Tariq and Ali seem like they would've made a terrific "Blade" together.-A.B.

item.title: Deno is joining Cloudflare
item.description: Deno is joining Cloudflare The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers. Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on celld to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog.) The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year: We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development. Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News: It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough. I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or network - it's an entirely new model for server development. My favorite feature of Deno has long been the permissions system, where you can run a Deno script and specify exactly which files and folders it can read and write to, and which network hosts it can access. Node.js has a similar permissions model these days, added in Node v20.0.0 in April 2023 and declared stable in Node v22.13.0 in January 2025. They don't yet support allow-listing specific network hosts though - networking is either on or off. Via Hacker News Tags: cloudfront, javascript, nodejs, ryan-dahl, sandboxing, deno

item.description: Everyone is very concerned about being respectable, so I'm going to be the goofball who raises worst-case possibilities. I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms. [...] The problem here is that the speed of AI producing surprises, and the speed of human beings replacing standards (even with the very best AI assistance) are just orders of magnitude different. You only recover from a surprise like this if you do the preparation in advance. - Matthew Green, on Twitter. I looked it up and Minicrypt is Russell Impagliazzo's hypothetical world in which public-key encryption is impossible. item.title: China's AI Model Race Is Just Getting More Crowded [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Imagine Epic Games, Apple and DoorDash were developing their own large language models now from scratch to compete against the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. That's basically what's happening in China, where a trio of big names from other parts of the tech industry have jumped into an already-crowded race to make cutting-edge AI. MiHoYo, a Shanghai-based videogame maker behind such hits like Genshin Impact, is developing its own LLMs with the goal of becoming a top-tier lab in China in the next couple of years. Xiaomi, a leading smartphone maker that also sells electric cars, released its latest LLM two weeks ago. And Meituan, China's biggest food delivery and local services app, in June unveiled a more powerful version of the LLM it launched last year.

item.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. Codex voice mode I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. Talking to my computer I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results. Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist. We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code. What we built We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice: A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for that Four working imports: The most recent Substack items via RSS Every other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried /api/v1/archive directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen Spinner All of my published monthly newsletters from my simonw/monthly-newsletter-archive GitHub repository My most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repository The /newsletters/ and /newsletters/2026/ public archive pages Newsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepage Weekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pages Integration with my site search engine It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while. Finishing it with a review Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request. I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead. You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR. I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR. The end result You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page, or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter. The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages. GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen. Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driver OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though. I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code. This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent. I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words. I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace! The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead. Tags: text-to-speech, ai, openai, generative-ai, llms, newsletter, coding-agents, codex, speech-to-text, site-upgrades
